title: Of first importance (1 Corinthians 15)
hook: Paul's summary, received and handed on: Christ died, was buried, was raised, appeared
tomorrow: how do you end a letter full of fights?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: all things edify, every gift taking its turn so the room is built up. Today Paul answers a bigger question: what comes first?

One box for a move. A phone with almost no storage left. Sooner or later everyone has to choose what to keep. Paul makes that choice about faith near the end of this letter, and his answer fits in one breath. "For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received." Received, then handed on, like something passed down a line of hands. So what made the cut?
screen: `ONE BOX. WHAT DO YOU KEEP?` → `FIRST OF ALL.` → `RECEIVED, THEN HANDED ON.`

segments.voice: Four lines: "how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures: And that he was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve." Died. Buried. Raised. Appeared. Then Paul lists witnesses: "above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present." Still around to be asked, he's saying. Last of all, himself. Why spell it out? Some in Corinth said there is no resurrection of the dead, and Paul won't soften it: "if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain." Now a neighbor. In Acts, Paul calls himself a Pharisee, on trial "of the hope and resurrection of the dead." That hope was Jewish before it was Christian, and it's still prayed. In the Amidah, a central Jewish prayer, one blessing praises God as the one who gives life to the dead. Shared ground: a God who brings life out of death. The honest difference: Paul says it has already begun, in one man. "But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept." Jewish tradition doesn't see that beginning in Jesus, and keeps the hope ahead. One hope, prayed in two houses, with a real difference about where it starts.
screen: `DIED, BURIED, RAISED, SEEN.` · `IF CHRIST BE NOT RISEN…` · `A HOPE PRAYED IN THE AMIDAH.` · `THE FIRSTFRUITS: BEGUN, OR AHEAD?` · then, large: `DIED, BURIED, RAISED, APPEARED.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper, or whatever's nearest. Write four words, one per line: died, buried, raised, appeared. Then read them back slowly, one breath each, letting each one land before the next, whether they're your words or, for now, simply Paul's.
Of first importance. Paul's own summary, received and handed on: Christ died, was buried, rose, and was seen.
Your line: died, buried, raised, appeared, four lines Paul received and then handed on. Until tomorrow.

fork.setup: you visit a friend's synagogue on Shabbat, and the prayer book praises God who gives life to the dead. your cousin whispers, 'wait, isn't that our line?' what's fair to say?

fork.reveal: Paul the Pharisee spoke of the hope and resurrection of the dead; the Amidah still praises God who gives life to the dead. the difference: Paul says it began in Christ, the firstfruits.

chat.meaning: Paul puts four lines first and says faith rests on them. You can share them honestly, as yours, without pressing anyone to agree.

Cephas.meaning: another name for Peter; it means a stone

Pharisee.meaning: a member of an ancient Jewish movement; Paul was one

Amidah.meaning: a central Jewish prayer, said standing

firstfruits.meaning: the first of the harvest, a promise of the rest

sources.ref: Amidah, second blessing (Gevurot): God 'who gives life to the dead' (mechayeh hametim)

notes: Wisdom day, unity thread: the shared ground is the hope of resurrection, in the neighbor's own words and source (the Amidah's second blessing, paraphrased as praising God 'who gives life to the dead'; Acts 23:6 for Paul as a Pharisee). The honest difference: Paul says it has begun in Christ, the firstfruits (15:20); Jewish tradition does not see that beginning in Jesus. Nothing is ranked and nothing is called 'the same'. A Jewish reader and a Christian Keeper should both confirm this is fair.

Some modern Jewish prayer books (e.g., Reform) word this blessing differently ('who gives life to all'); the lesson says 'in the Amidah' without claiming every prayer book. A Keeper may want 'in the traditional Amidah'.
The index hook says 'the earliest summary'; the lesson makes no claim about its date or that it is the earliest; it says only that Paul 'received' it and handed it on (15:3).
The index carry is 'died, buried, raised, appeared'; the KJV has 'died... buried... rose again... was seen'. The carry is kept as the index has it.
The KJV's 'first of all' (ἐν πρώτοις) is rendered 'of first importance' in other translations; games.original notes both. Confirm.
Gloss 'Cephas... it means a stone' follows John 1:42 ('Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone').
